Title: A Highway of Water
Content: In `1849`, travelers going from the East Coast to the West Coast of the United States had `text(two)` choices. They could go by wagon across America's sometimes dangerous prairie land. The other choice was to board a sailing ship in New York bound for California. This route led down the Atlantic Coast, around the tip of South America into the Pacific Ocean, and then north up the Pacific Coast to California. The `text(15,000 mile)` journey took `text(months)`. Severe weather, which is common at the tip of South America where the `text(two)` oceans meet, could add as much as `text(five months)` more to the trip.

Could there be any other way to travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific? The answer was a canal. A canal is a man-made waterway. It provides passage between `text(two)` natural bodies of water. Think of a canal as a highway of water.

Panama is a small country connecting North America with South America. At its narrowest part, it is barely `text(fifty miles)` wide. The Atlantic Ocean is on the eastern side of Panama, and the Pacific Ocean is on the western side. Panama seemed the logical place to build a canal. With a canal in Panama, the trip from New York to California would be `text(8,000 miles)` shorter than sailing around South America. Travel time could be `text(three months)` instead of `text(eight months)`.

In `1879`, France began to build a canal across Panama. Problems began as soon as construction started. It rained `text(every day)`, causing the soil to become heavy and gooey. Temperatures climbed as high as `text(130 degrees)`. `text(Two)` diseases, yellow fever and malaria, caused illness or death to the majority of workers. In `1899`, France `ultext(abandoned)` the project.

The U.S. Congress decided to finish the canal. The U.S. government paid `text($40 million)` to France for the completed work and abandoned equipment. A treaty was signed guaranteeing Panama `text($250,000 each year)` for use of the land. In November `1904`, American workers began completion of the Panama Canal.

American officials wanted to protect workers from disease. An engineer, Frank Stevens, arrived at the work camp in Panama. He began building hospitals as well as water and sewage systems. He supported the camp doctor's efforts to fight mosquitoes, the cause of malaria and yellow fever. More than `text(100 tons)` of insect powder was ordered, and crews set about eliminating mosquitoes.

A system of locks and gates had to be built in the canal to move ships from `text(one)` ocean to the other. A lock is a giant box made of concrete. A ship must pass through `text(three)` locks in the Panama Canal. `text(Each lock)` holds `text(millions of gallons)` of water. A ship moves into a lock, which is filled with water. Water is pumped into the lock or out of the lock. This raises or lowers the ship to the level of water in the next lock. The gates open, and the ship moves into the next lock.

By `text(early 1913)`, the canal was nearly complete. It took several `text(months)` to fill the canal with water. On `text(September 26, 1913)`, an old tugboat was the `text(first)` ship through the canal. `text(Thousands)` of people watched and cheered. The locks worked perfectly.

In modern times, more than `text(15,000)` ships make the `text(fifty-mile)` trip through the canal `text(each year)`. `text(Each ship)` that passes through must pay a fee based on its size. A ship called Radiance of the Seas paid the largest fee ever, which was `$201,177`. The smallest fee was collected in `1928`, when Richard Halliburton paid `$0.36` to swim through the canal.
Time, money, and possibly even lives have been saved as ships use the shorter route from ocean to ocean provided by the canal. The Panama Canal, a highway of water, is a phenomenon.
